metadata.title: Limited Sensitivity of Ultrasound‐Guided Fine‐Needle Aspiration Cytology for Occult Nodal Metastases in Early‐Stage Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

sections.text: ABSTRACT Background Ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration cytology (US‐FNAC) is commonly used in the diagnostic work‐up of head and neck cancer, but its ability to detect occult lymph node metastases in early‐stage oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) with a clinically negative neck remains unclear. Methods A retrospective analysis was performed in 578 patients with early‐stage OSCC (cT1‐3N0) who underwent US‐FNAC prior to surgery. Histopathology, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and follow‐up were used as reference standards. Results Occult nodal metastases were found in 179 patients (31.0%). US‐FNAC showed low sensitivity (15.9%) and a negative predictive value of 72.9%, resulting in 149 false‐negative cases (25.8%). Specificity (99.5%) and positive predictive value (90.3%) were high, with only 2 false‐positive results. Conclusions In patients with early‐stage oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma and a clinically negative neck, US‐FNAC demonstrates high specificity but limited sensitivity and negative predictive value. These findings indicate that US‐FNAC alone is insufficient to exclude occult nodal metastases and should be regarded as an adjunctive diagnostic tool rather than a stand‐alone nodal staging strategy.

Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), along with other head and neck squamous cell carcinomas, frequently metastasizes via the lymphatic system. In early‐stage OSCC, the incidence of occult lymph node metastases ranges from 21% to 35% [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ]. Clinical staging of the neck begins with palpation, followed by various imaging modalities, including computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), 18 F‐fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography‐computed tomography (FDG‐PET/CT), ultrasonography, and ultrasound‐guided fine‐needle aspiration cytology (US‐FNAC) [ 8 , 9 ]. In the Netherlands, US‐FNAC has become a standardized diagnostic imaging modality for staging the neck in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma since the late 1980s [ 10 ]. This diagnostic technique combines the potentially high radiological sensitivity of ultrasonography with the pathological specificity of cytological assessment [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ]. A systematic review reported excellent accuracy of US‐FNAC, with a mean sensitivity of 80% (95% CI: 57%–92%) and a mean specificity of 98% (95% CI: 93%–99.7%) for detecting lymph node metastases in head and neck cancer. However, the studied patients were clinically suspicious for lymph node metastases [ 13 ]. There are no large, high‐quality studies investigating the diagnostic accuracy of US‐FNAC in the clinically negative neck. Reported sensitivity rates for US‐FNAC vary widely, ranging from 19% to 76%, in patients with clinically negative necks [ 10 , 15 , 16 ]. Therefore, the specific value of the US‐FNAC in detecting occult metastases in early‐stage OSCC remains unclear [ 10 , 15 , 16 , 17 ]. In current practice, following a negative US‐FNAC result, patients in our institute would undergo a sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). Before 2014, these patients would instead have received an elective neck dissection. A positive US‐FNAC result would lead to immediate therapeutic neck dissection, eliminating the need for an SLNB and therefore avoiding a subsequent second surgical procedure, such as a therapeutic neck dissection after a positive SLNB. However, the value of US‐FNAC in clinical practice may depend on its diagnostic accuracy in early‐stage OSCC patients. Our study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of US‐FNAC in detecting occult lymphatic metastases in patients presenting with early‐stage OSCC and to determine its value in the current diagnostic workup.

This study abided by the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University Medical Center Utrecht (reference number 25U‐0236). The Internal Review Board waived the requirement for signed informed consent forms for all subjects. Samples and data were handled according to the General Data Protection Regulation.

A retrospective study was conducted on patients with early‐stage OSCC and clinically negative neck (cT1‐3 N0) when T3 is defined based on tumor dimensions of > 2 cm and ≤ 4 cm with a depth of invasion > 10 mm, according to the TNM Staging System of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) 8th Edition [ 18 ]. A clinically negative neck was defined as the absence of palpable enlarged cervical lymph nodes, while occult lymph node metastases were defined as metastases present (but not yet detected) in this clinically negative neck. All patients underwent an ultrasound of the neck (with or without FNAC) before transoral excision of the primary tumor. Patients with a history of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, as well as those receiving primary (chemo)radiotherapy or elective postoperative radiation therapy of the neck, were excluded. Patients with a negative SLNB or those managed with a wait‐and‐scan strategy were followed for a minimum of 24 months postoperatively, to confirm a true‐negative nodal status. Patients who developed a second primary tumor or local recurrence during follow‐up were censored at the time of diagnosis.

All patients were ultrasonographically examined by a radiologist consultant, a supervised resident, or a dedicated technician. With a 5–12 MHz linear array transducer (Model EPIQ 5 or EPIQ 7; Philips Medical Systems, Eindhoven, The Netherlands), bilateral screening of the neck was performed from levels I through VI. The maximum short‐axis diameter (mm) of cervical lymph nodes was measured, and the presence of suspicious morphological features in the lymph nodes was assessed. Cytological aspiration was performed when a normal lymph node had a short‐axis diameter of ≥ 5 mm in levels I, III, IV, V, or VI, or ≥ 7 mm in level II. If one or more suspicious morphological criteria were present during ultrasonography, aspiration was also attempted irrespective of the size [ 19 ]. Fine‐needle aspiration cytology was performed exclusively in lymph nodes that were considered suspicious on ultrasonography; FNAC results were therefore not available for lymph nodes without an indication for FNAC. Suspicious morphological features included: the absence of a fatty hilus; focal cortical widening; round shape (short (S)/long (L) > 0.5); irregular reflection patterns; hypoechoic lymph node; intranodal cystic necrosis; or vascular changes on color Doppler. Aspiration of these lymph nodes was performed with a 10 mL syringe and a 0.8 mm × 40 mm needle. At maximum, two suspicious lymph nodes were selected for cytological aspiration per side. The number of aspiration attempts per node varied from one to three.

For each aspirate, a cytological smear was prepared and stained using May‐Grunwald‐Giemsa solution. All smears were thoroughly examined by a cytotechnologist and a cytopathologist. Cytopathological findings were classified into the following categories: (1) non‐representative , (2) benign/reactive , (3) suspicious for malignancy , and (4) malignant . Categories (3) suspicious for malignancy , and (4) malignant were classified as positive, category (2) benign/reactive was considered negative. For category (1) non‐representative a repeat aspiration was recommended. A US‐FNAC was considered positive if atypical epithelial cells suspicious for malignancy or definitive malignant cells were identified. It was considered negative if only lymphoid cells were identified or when no cytological aspiration was performed due to the absence of suspicious lymph nodes. If no repeat cytological aspiration was performed following a non‐representative result, the outcome of the multidisciplinary team meeting was taken into account. During the multidisciplinary team meeting, the entire US‐FNAC procedure was reviewed, including the presence or absence of suspicious lymph nodes, as well as the overall clinical and radiological context. Despite the insufficient cytopathological result, the case was classified according to the most likely outcome—either positive or negative.

Patients with positive US‐FNAC findings underwent subsequent neck dissection, whereas US‐FNAC‐negative patients—defined as patients for whom no indication for FNAC was present and patients with a negative FNAC result—were managed using one of three strategies: a wait‐and‐scan strategy, an SLNB, or an elective neck dissection. Since October 2014, the SLNB procedure has been implemented as the preferred nodal staging strategy for early stage OSCC at our institution, replacing elective neck dissection and improving patient selection for a wait‐and‐scan strategy. However, its clinical implementation occurred progressively and was not uniform for all eligible patients immediately after introduction. The choice of nodal management strategy during this period was influenced by logistical availability, multidisciplinary team decision‐making, tumor‐related characteristics, and patient‐related factors. If metastases were identified in the sentinel lymph node, an additional neck dissection was performed as a second surgical procedure. Before October 2014, patients with a radiological depth of invasion of the primary tumor estimated at 4 mm or more typically underwent elective neck dissection. Patients managed with the wait‐and‐scan strategy underwent strict postoperative follow‐up, including physical examination and US‐FNAC every 3 months during the first year. Patients with a negative SLNB or managed with a wait‐and‐scan strategy were followed for a minimum of 24 months.

All patients underwent surgical resection of the primary tumor. Subsequently, postoperative radiotherapy was given based on resection margin status and the presence of unfavorable tumor characteristics, such as worst pattern of invasion category 4 or 5 [ 20 ], perineural invasion, and/or angioinvasion.

Histopathological assessment of resected lymph nodes, as well as nodal status during follow‐up, was used as the reference standard. Detected cervical metastases were classified histopathologically according to TNM Staging System of the UICC 8th Edition [ 18 ]: isolated tumor cells (ITC) for metastases smaller than 0.2 mm, micrometastases for those measuring between 0.2 mm and 2.0 mm, and macrometastases for those larger than 2.0 mm. According to the TNM Staging System, the presence of ITC is classified as pN0 [ 18 ]. However, in line with the SENT‐trial by Schilling et al. [ 5 ], patients with ITC were managed as having a positive neck. To ensure true‐negative nodal status, patients with a negative SLNB or managed with a wait‐and‐scan strategy were monitored for at least 24 months. Follow‐up was censored at the time of diagnosis in cases of local recurrence or a second primary tumor.

All data were obtained from original diagnostic reports from the electronic patient records. The diagnostic accuracy of US‐FNAC was assessed using results of US‐FNAC and histopathological examination of lymph nodes and complementary neck dissection specimens, along with follow‐up data as the reference standard. To evaluate diagnostic accuracy, true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN) were first defined: True positives (TP): Cases correctly identified as positive—patients with a positive FNAC result and histopathological confirmation of a cervical metastasis in neck dissection. True negatives (TN): Cases correctly identified as negative—patients managed with a wait‐and‐scan strategy who had a negative follow‐up, patients with a negative SLNB histopathology result and negative follow‐up, and patients with a negative US(‐FNAC) result confirmed by a negative histopathological assessment of elective neck dissection and negative follow‐up. False positives (FP): Cases incorrectly identified as positive—patients with a positive US‐FNAC result but without histopathological confirmation of a metastasis. False negatives (FN): Cases incorrectly identified as negative—patients with a negative US(‐FNAC) result but with histopathological evidence of a metastasis in SLN or neck dissection, or those in whom a regional metastasis was detected during follow‐up, provided there was no local recurrence or second primary tumor. From these values, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated per patient as follows. Sensitivity: TP/(TP + FN), specificity: TN/(FP + TN), PPV: TP/(TP + FP), and NPV: TN/(TN + FN). Data analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 29.0.1. Categorical variables are presented as the number of cases and percentages. Continuous variables with a parametric distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), while non‐parametric variables are presented as median with interquartile range (IQR).

From January 2012 to November 2022, a total of 578 patients with early‐stage OSCC were retrospectively included in the study. The median follow‐up was 48 months (IQR 28–62). Number of patients per neck treatment strategy is presented in Figure 1 . Patient and tumor characteristics, stratified by neck treatment strategy, are summarized in Table 1 . The majority of patients presented with OSCC of the oral tongue (54%) and most tumors were classified as cT1 (54%). Histopathological characteristics for each neck treatment strategy are presented in Table 2 . Among all included patients, 30% were found to have occult cervical metastases, which included 8% classified as false‐negative cases where metastases were identified during follow‐up. Of all included patients 48 (8%) had pathological lymph nodes with extranodal extension (ENE), defined as extension of viable tumor outside the lymph node into the perinodal soft tissue [ 21 ]. Among these pathological lymph nodes with ENE, FNAC was performed in 33 cases (69%), of which 21 cases were reported as positive and 1 case as inconclusive. Eleven lymph nodes with ENE were missed despite FNAC being performed, in addition to 15 lymph nodes where no FNAC was performed at all. In total, pathological lymph nodes with ENE were not detected by US‐FNAC in 26 of 48 cases (54%). Table 3 summarizes the results of US‐FNAC. FNAC was performed in 42% of patients (242/587), assessing a total of 315 lymph nodes. A positive US‐FNAC was observed in 12%, while 4% of all FNACs were inconclusive. The sensitivity and NPV of US‐FNAC were 16% and 73%, respectively. There were two false‐positive cases, in which cytological assessment indicated positive results, but no metastases were found in the subsequent neck dissection specimens or during follow‐up. Additionally, there were 149 false‐negative US‐FNAC cases. When stratified by clinical T‐stage, the NPV of US‐FNAC decreased from 82% in cT1 to 67% in cT2 and 65% in cT3 tumors. The corresponding PPV values were 95%, 86%, and 100%, respectively (Table 4 ). The characteristics of the lymph nodes selected for US‐FNAC are summarized in Table 5 .

This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of US‐FNAC in detecting occult lymphatic metastases in early‐stage OSCC. Among 578 patients, 179 patients had occult lymph node metastases of which 28 were detected with US‐FNAC. US‐FNAC demonstrated a high specificity (99%) and PPV (90%), but low sensitivity (16%) and a NPV (73%). False‐negatives were observed in 149 cases. The findings underscore US‐FNAC's limitations in evaluating the clinically negative neck but reaffirm its utility for immediate therapeutic planning in positive cases. While limited sensitivity of US‐FNAC has been described in earlier, smaller studies, the present analysis, representing the largest cohort to date, allows for a more robust and generalizable assessment of its diagnostic performance in early‐stage oral cavity cancer. A key limitation of US‐FNAC in detecting occult lymph node metastases is that ultrasound can only visualize metastases once they have altered the size or morphology of the lymph node. This implies that only relatively advanced metastases are detectable, while smaller ones are likely to be missed. Consequently, the majority of existing metastases may remain undetected with US‐FNAC. In addition, diagnostic accuracy may be further limited by sampling error due to the presence of micrometastases in unaspirated areas of the lymph node, as well as by misinterpretation or insufficient cytological material for adequate assessment [ 21 ]. Criteria for US‐FNAC in patients with OSCC and a clinically negative neck are based on size and morphological characteristics of the cervical lymph nodes, consisting of the absence of an echogenic hilus, presence of cystic or coagulation necrosis, presence of abnormal vessels, presence of eccentric cortical hypertrophy, and hypo‐echoic sonomorphology [ 14 , 22 , 23 ]. Selection of the lymph node to be aspirated may be challenging as these morphological criteria for lymph node evaluation are often not applicable to smaller lymph nodes [ 24 ]. The sensitivity of US‐FNAC in this study appears lower than previously published reports, where sensitivity in patients with a clinically negative neck ranged from 18% to 39% as reported by Borgmeester et al. [ 15 ], 42% by Takes et al. [ 16 ] 50% by Righi et al. [ 17 ] and 76% by van den Brekel et al. [ 10 ]. Several factors may explain this discrepancy. First, other studies included all head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. Notably, Borgemeester et al. provided separate sensitivity rates for US‐FNAC based on primary tumor location, with the lowest sensitivity reported for the oral cavity (27%), followed by the oropharynx (50%) and the larynx (54%). They observed that ultrasonography was more challenging in level I lymph nodes, a region where metastases from the oral cavity tumors are more common compared to other primary tumor sites [ 15 ]. Additionally, the inclusion of larger tumors, with clinical T‐stage cT3 and cT4 in earlier studies likely contributed to the higher incidence of regional metastases, reported to range between 38% and 47% in these populations [ 10 , 15 , 16 , 17 ]. In these older studies, clinical staging was based on the 7th edition of the TNM classification, in which cT3 corresponds to a primary tumor size greater than 4 cm. In our study, we used the 8th edition of the TNM classification and exclusively included patients with primary tumors smaller than 4 cm. In our study, the incidence of cervical metastases was 31%, consistent with earlier studies focusing on similar study populations [ 3 , 4 , 25 , 26 ]. Furthermore, larger tumors often harbor larger metastases, and therefore are relatively more easy detectable by imaging modalities [ 27 , 28 ]. It should be noted that the a priori probability of lymph node metastasis increases with advancing clinical T stage. As such, both the PPV and, more notably, the NPV of US‐FNAC are likely to be affected by this underlying difference in metastatic risk, particularly in patients with cT3 tumors. Although the negative predictive value of US‐FNAC was higher in patients with cT1 tumors compared with more advanced disease, an NPV exceeding 80% still implies that a clinically relevant proportion of occult nodal metastases would remain undetected if US‐FNAC were used as a stand‐alone strategy. Therefore, a negative US‐FNAC result alone appears insufficient to reliably exclude nodal disease, even in early‐stage (cT1) oral cavity cancer. Only one study by Chaturvedi et al. investigated a similar population to ours and showed an evenly low sensitivity value of 14% for the US‐FNAC [ 26 ]. This study included only patients with OSCC and classified as cT1 or cT2, according to the 7th edition of the TNM classification. However, neck dissection was used as the reference standard, rather than SLNB. In addition, ITCs were not reported, and the study did not include a minimum follow‐up period of 2 years. Interpretation of a positive US‐FNAC varied in one study. Borgemeester et al. considered an ultrasound result with evident suspicion of metastases as positive, even in the absence of cytological confirmation [ 15 ]. In contrast, our study defined US‐FNAC as positive only when cytology confirmed the ultrasound findings of metastatic disease, which influences the sensitivity rate. Lastly, our study utilized a combined reference standard of histopathological examination and follow‐up. Incorporating follow‐up provides a more representative reference standard than histopathology alone, as it accounts for skip metastases and metastases in surgically untreated neck sides. Moreover, occult lymph nodes metastases, which may be missed in up to 16% of cases using routine histopathological examination of neck dissection specimens, are likely to become clinically manifest in an untreated neck during follow‐up [ 29 , 30 , 31 ]. In contrast, previous studies relied solely on histopathological examination of neck dissection specimens as the reference standard. This approach can result in higher sensitivity rates for US‐FNAC by failing to detect occult metastases that only become clinically evident during follow‐up. The primary limitation of US‐FNAC lies in its inability to detect and accurately select the appropriate lymph node for aspiration. In our study population, the criteria for aspiration were predominantly node size, followed by round shape, absence of a fatty hilus, cortical widening, hypo‐echoic lymph nodes, intranodal cystic necrosis, or vascular changes on color Doppler. However, the median size difference between positive and negative lymph nodes was only 1 mm, highlighting the challenge of relying on size as a sole criterion. Sampling error of the cytological aspirate is a well‐recognized limitation of US‐FNAC in detecting micrometastases [ 32 , 33 ]. In this study, histopathological assessment revealed macrometastases as the largest tumor deposit in 86 (15%) patients, micrometastases in 41 (7%) patients and ITC in 3 (0.5%) patients. In our study, ITC were managed as indicative of a positive neck. Two patients received adjuvant treatment of the neck: one underwent radiotherapy, and the other a subsequent neck dissection. Following multidisciplinary discussion, the third patient opted for a wait‐and‐scan strategy instead of an adjuvant neck dissection. In our study population, US‐FNAC primarily identified advanced lymphatic metastases, underscoring its limited sensitivity for detecting smaller metastatic deposits. In our study, US‐FNAC procedures were performed by various radiologist consultants, introducing a potential for higher inter‐observer variability. Knappe et al. demonstrated a learning curve among radiologists, with improvement in both examination efficiency and diagnostic yield over time. Specifically, their study reported a reduction in examination time from 45 min to approximately 15 min and a decrease in non‐diagnostic aspirates from 22% to 8% during a 2‐year period [ 34 ]. van den Brekel et al. reported the highest sensitivity rate of 73% for US‐FNAC in evaluating the clinically negative neck [ 11 ]. This prospective study was conducted in a highly controlled setting, and all procedures were performed by a single clinician, suggesting that an experienced consultant might enhance US‐FNAC sensitivity. These findings suggest that inter‐observer variation and the radiologist's experience level may significantly influence the sensitivity of US‐FNAC. While the role of a learning curve in improving diagnostic accuracy remains unclear, the variability observed underscores the importance of standardization and training in optimizing the performance of US‐FNAC in clinical practice. Since 2014, SLNB has been routinely performed at our institution as a diagnostic staging modality for patients with early‐stage OSCC and a clinically negative neck. SLNB demonstrates high accuracy in detecting lymphatic metastases, including micrometastases [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 25 ]. The potential value of US‐FNAC in the current diagnostic workflow lies in its ability to detect metastases prior to the SLNB procedure. By detecting metastatic lymph nodes prior to SLNB, US‐FNAC could eliminate the need for this additional invasive diagnostic procedure, and allow for direct therapeutic neck dissection avoiding a second staged surgical procedure. Given the low sensitivity of US‐FNAC, improvements can be made through more precise lymph node selection. Sensitivity may increase when targeted US‐FNAC is performed on sentinel lymph nodes. Several innovative techniques could aid in identifying and targeting sentinel lymph nodes during ultrasonography. Notable examples include the fusion of handheld SPECT–CT with ultrasound and the use of microbubbles with contrast‐enhanced ultrasonography. Both methods have been technically successful in selecting sentinel lymph nodes in the neck and axilla [ 35 , 36 , 37 ]. However, applying microbubbles in the complex anatomy of the head and neck poses additional challenges compared to the axilla. Further studies are necessary to evaluate the potential added value of these techniques.

In this large cohort of patients with OSCC and clinically negative necks, US‐FNAC demonstrated high specificity but limited sensitivity and negative predictive value. Even in a population with a relatively low pre‐test probability of nodal disease, a negative US‐FNAC result alone was insufficient to reliably exclude occult lymph node metastases. US‐FNAC may be valuable as an adjunctive diagnostic tool to support immediate therapeutic decision‐making in patients with positive findings; however, its limitations should be carefully considered when used for nodal staging in early‐stage disease.
Informed consent was waived according to this assessment.
